interactions.label: Why does haematogenous osteomyelitis in children preferentially localise to the

params.question: Why does haematogenous osteomyelitis in children preferentially localise to the metaphysis of long bones?

answers.text: The metaphysis has the thinnest cortex, making it most vulnerable to direct bacterial invasion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cortical thickness does not determine the site of haematogenous seeding. The metaphysis is targeted because of its unique vascular anatomy, not cortical weakness.

answers.text: Sinusoidal vascular loops in the metaphysis slow blood flow and reduce local phagocytic activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Sluggish flow through the sinusoidal loops allows bacteria to settle and multiply, while reduced phagocytic capacity limits early clearance of organisms.

answers.text: The growth plate traps circulating bacteria, concentrating them in the adjacent metaphysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The growth plate acts as a barrier to the spread of established infection, but it does not trap circulating bacteria. Initial localisation depends on the vascular loops, not the growth plate's barrier function.

answers.text: The metaphyseal periosteum is loosely attached, facilitating early subperiosteal abscess formation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Loose periosteal attachment allows subperiosteal abscess spread once infection is established, but it does not explain why bacteria initially lodge in the metaphysis rather than elsewhere.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key is the vascular anatomy. Sinusoidal loops in the metaphysis slow blood flow and impair phagocytic clearance, creating a protected niche where bacteria — most commonly Staphylococcus aureus — can establish infection.
Exactly right. The sinusoidal vascular loops create a zone of sluggish flow and impaired phagocytosis, which is why Staphylococcus aureus seeds the metaphysis in 80–90% of childhood osteomyelitis.

interactions.label: In Paget disease of bone, serum alkaline phosphatase peaks during the initial os

params.question: In Paget disease of bone, serum alkaline phosphatase peaks during the initial osteolytic phase when osteoclast activity is highest.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. Alkaline phosphatase is secreted by osteoblasts, not osteoclasts. It peaks during the mixed phase when both cell types are hyperactive and osteoblast activity reaches its zenith — sometimes 10–20 times above normal. In the osteolytic phase, the marker that rises is urinary hydroxyproline, a collagen breakdown product reflecting osteoclast-driven resorption.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Alkaline phosphatase is an osteoblast enzyme, so it peaks during the mixed phase when osteoblasts are maximally hyperactive alongside osteoclasts, not during the purely osteolytic phase. Urinary hydroxyproline, a collagen breakdown marker, is the one that rises in the osteolytic phase.

params.question: A 16-year-old boy presents with a painful swelling just above the knee. X-ray shows a mixed lytic-sclerotic metaphyseal lesion with a sunburst pattern and periosteal elevation at the tumour margin. Which biopsy finding confirms the diagnosis?

answers.text: Sheets of small round blue cells that are strongly CD99-positive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern characterises Ewing sarcoma, which targets the diaphysis in younger children and shows an onion-skin periosteal reaction — not the sunburst pattern and metaphyseal location described here.

answers.text: Multinucleated giant cells with nuclei identical to the surrounding stromal cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes giant cell tumour of bone, an epiphyseal lesion in adults aged 20–40 with a soap-bubble lytic pattern — a different age group, location, and radiological appearance.

answers.text: Lace-like pink osteoid matrix produced directly by pleomorphic sarcomatous cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Malignant osteoid — pink, amorphous, lace-like matrix deposited by tumour cells — is the single defining histological feature of osteosarcoma.

answers.text: A hyaline cartilage cap overlying a bony excrescence with cortical and medullary continuity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes osteochondroma, the most common benign bone tumour. It forms a cartilage-capped outgrowth, not a destructive metaphyseal mass.

overallFeedback.feedback: The defining feature is malignant osteoid — lace-like pink matrix produced directly by pleomorphic sarcomatous cells. This single finding distinguishes osteosarcoma from every other primary bone tumour.

Well analysed. Malignant osteoid is the histological feature that defines osteosarcoma. Combined with the clinical triad — adolescent age, metaphyseal knee location, and sunburst pattern — the diagnosis is definitive.

interactions.label: A patient presents with symmetric swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proxim

params.question: A patient presents with symmetric swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, morning stiffness lasting over one hour, and marginal erosions without osteophytes on X-ray. The distal interphalangeal joints are completely spared. Which pathological process drives this pattern of joint destruction?

answers.text: Mechanical stress triggering chondrocyte release of metalloproteinases, leading to cartilage fibrillation and eburnation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes osteoarthritis, which favours weight-bearing joints and characteristically involves the distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden's nodes) — the very joints spared in this presentation.

answers.text: Neutrophilic inflammation triggered by engulfment of negatively birefringent needle-shaped urate crystals

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the mechanism of acute gout, which classically targets the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) as an acute monoarthritis — not a symmetric polyarthritis with morning stiffness.

answers.text: Chronic tophaceous crystal deposition with foreign-body giant cell reaction eroding periarticular bone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes chronic tophaceous gout. Tophi are masses of urate crystals surrounded by giant cells, but they produce an asymmetric pattern, not the symmetric MCP/PIP involvement with DIP sparing seen here.

answers.text: Pannus formation driven by a TNF/IL-1/IL-6 cytokine cascade from HLA-DR4-mediated autoimmune synovitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. CD4-positive T cells recognise citrullinated peptides presented by HLA-DR4 in the synovium, triggering a cytokine cascade that generates pannus — destructive granulation tissue that erodes cartilage and bone in a symmetric small-joint pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: The clinical pattern — symmetric small-joint arthritis with DIP sparing, morning stiffness exceeding one hour, and marginal erosions without osteophytes — defines rheumatoid arthritis. The destructive agent is pannus, granulation tissue generated by an HLA-DR4-driven cytokine cascade of TNF, IL-1, and IL-6.

Well analysed. The symmetric MCP/PIP involvement, DIP sparing, prolonged morning stiffness, and marginal erosions without osteophytes define rheumatoid arthritis. Pannus — driven by TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 — is the tissue that mediates joint destruction.
